cards.title: A space probe discovered its own memory leak millions of miles from Earth
cards.body: In 2002, NASA engineers realized the Deep Space 1 probe was losing memory. Its on-board software was leaking data buffers, slowly starving the spacecraft of RAM. Rather than letting it crash, engineers wrote and uploaded a remote patch while the probe was 200 million miles away. It successfully reclaimed lost memory and allowed Deep Space 1 to complete its extended mission to comet Borrelly.

cards.title: A single print command sparked the creation of PostScript and Adobe
cards.body: In the late 1970s at Xerox PARC, John Warnock and Chuck Geschke developed 'Interpress' to describe pages for laser printers with mathematical precision. When Xerox refused to commercialize it quickly, the two computer scientists quit in 1982 to launch Adobe. They rebuilt the concept as PostScript, a Turing-complete programming language that revolutionized desktop publishing by treating every letter and graphic as executable code.

cards.title: The father of the computer mouse used a block of wood and two wheels
cards.body: In 1964, Douglas Engelbart and Bill English built the world's first computer mouse at the Stanford Research Institute. Carved from a hollowed-out block of carved wood, it housed two perpendicular metal wheels that tracked movement across a desk. Patented as an 'X-Y position indicator for a display system,' SRI nicknamed it 'mouse' because the cord trailing out the back resembled a tail.

cards.title: Ken Thompson built Unix's core text editor in just one week
cards.body: In 1969, Ken Thompson sat down to write a text editor for the fledgeling Unix operating system. Borrowing ideas from the earlier QED editor, he created 'ed' in less than a week. Designed for slow teletype terminals that printed on physical rolls of paper, ed kept output to an absolute minimum—often responding to syntax errors with nothing more than a cryptic question mark.

sources.title: An Overview of the ed Text Editor

cards.title: The fast inverse square root constant remained an enigma for years
cards.body: When id Software open-sourced Quake III Arena in 2005, developers marveled at a bizarre C function that calculated 1/√x up to four times faster than hardware division. The algorithm used the mysterious hexadecimal constant 0x5F3759DF to seed a brilliant bit-level floating-point approximation. Despite widespread attribution to John Carmack, the trick originated decades earlier among engineers at Ardent Computer.

quizzes.question: How did NASA fix the memory leak threatening Deep Space 1 in 2002?
options: By uploading a remote software patch across millions of miles
By switching to a backup analog control unit
By forcing an ungraceful hardware restart from ground control
By relying on an autonomous AI self-repair routine
quizzes.explanation: NASA engineers remotely beamed a patch across 200 million miles of space to fix the spacecraft's buffer leak.

quizzes.question: What kind of language is PostScript technically classified as?
options: A plain-text markup language like Markdown
quizzes.explanation: PostScript is a full, Turing-complete stack-based programming language, not just a static graphics description.

quizzes.question: What material was used to encase Douglas Engelbart's first prototype mouse in 1964?
quizzes.explanation: The original 1964 prototype built at SRI International was carved from a block of wood with two tracking wheels.

quizzes.question: Why did the original Unix text editor 'ed' produce extremely terse error messages?
options: It was designed for slow paper teletype printers
The computer ran out of memory for string constants
Unix had an operating system limit of 1-character errors
quizzes.explanation: Printing onto physical paper teletypes was slow and wasted paper, so ed printed only '?' on errors.

quizzes.question: Who actually authored the original fast inverse square root algorithm popularized in Quake III?
quizzes.explanation: While popularized by John Carmack in Quake III, the algorithm originated with Greg Walsh and Cleve Moler at Ardent Computer.

guesses.prompt: How many millions of miles away from Earth was Deep Space 1 when engineers successfully patched its memory leak?
guesses.explanation: Engineers beamed the software fix over 200 million miles across the solar system.

misconceptions.claim: John Carmack invented the famous fast inverse square root algorithm found in Quake III's source code.
misconceptions.explanation: Carmack included the code in Quake III, but the trick was actually developed in the late 1980s by engineers at Ardent Computer.

misconceptions.claim: PostScript files are just static vector images, not full computer programs.
misconceptions.explanation: PostScript is a complete, Turing-complete programming language with loops, conditionals, and variables.
